entries.title: Republicans Want to Flip the Script on Health Care
entries.summary: Polling finds public trust swinging hard toward Democrats on controlling costs, but some GOP candidates see an opening.
entries.content:
Back in the summer, physician and former Republican Rep. Brad Wenstrup and Trump-aligned pollster John McLaughlin offered coaching to House Republicans on how to talk about health care: Lean in.

Republican strategists say the party has treated the topic as Democratic turf for years, and such advice may sound counterintuitive a year after Republicans passed $1 trillion in federal health care budget cuts.

But some GOP lawmakers are taking it, running ads on targeted health care subjects in swing districts in states like Iowa, New York and New Jersey, where candidates and strategists recognize they need an affirmative response — especially as open-enrollment season opens this month for millions of Americans.

Wenstrup and McLaughlin explained why in briefings to the National Republican Congressional Committee and the Republican Study Committee that offered polling data that pegged health insurance costs as voters’ leading health care concern.

The data also suggested ways to push back. One McLaughlin & Associates survey of 2,000 likely voters commissioned by Americans for Health Excellence, which Wenstrup leads, said 65% of voters were more likely to vote for a Republican candidate who supports cracking down on fraud, waste and abuse by insurance companies.

“Our polling shows common-sense pocketbook solutions have support from more than eight in ten voters, including strong majorities of Republicans, Democrats and Independents,” Wenstrup said in a statement to The Washington Sun. “That is not just good policy. It is winning ground for candidates and smart to work on behalf of patients.”

While campaigns are likely making their own decisions, such ideas are being promoted in competitive districts.

Rep. Mike Lawler of New York has highlighted affordability in his ads. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa pledged to take on “Big Insurance” companies, as did Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate. Rep. Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey has focused on ensuring patients have equal access to physical and mental health care through their insurance coverage.

For Republicans in competitive districts, campaigning on health care offers an opportunity to reach beyond their usual voters, said Kristin Davison, a national Republican consultant at Axiom Strategies.

“It's also something that gives a permission slip to someone that's not used to voting Republican to consider you because you're talking about an issue that Republicans haven't necessarily dominated in the past,” Davison said.

Rob Burgess, CEO of Connector, Inc. and a national Republican strategist, described the shift as Republicans becoming more willing to compete on the issue.

“Here is the pivotal shift: Republicans have stopped playing defense,” Burgess said. “For years our side treated health care as the other team's turf and hoped the subject wouldn't come up.”

Burgess argued that the pressure starts with candidates hearing about affordability in their districts.

“Those members aren't following a memo. They're following their voters, and the party is catching up to what they already know,” he said.

Sarah Chamberlain, the president of the Republican Main Street Partnership, also said the new messaging on health care is not a broader Republican strategy but reflects more of a district-by-district approach. She pointed to Kean, who has publicly discussed his own mental health struggles, as an example of a candidate whose personal experience shapes his health care priorities.

Lawler, who has long discussed health care, told The Sun in an interview that he helped block proposals to reduce the federal government’s share of Medicaid funding and negotiated an extension of New York’s tax on managed care organizations, which he said preserved $1.2 billion for the state’s hospital system.

Lawler was also one of four Republicans who signed a discharge petition to force a vote to extend enhanced Affordable Care Act marketplace insurance subsidies for three years. The bill passed the House but ultimately stalled in the Senate.

Such efforts and ads, however, are running into some on-the-ground reality that millions of Americans are about to encounter as the annual process of updating insurance choices starts later this month.

Open enrollment for Medicare recipients starts Oct. 15. Shopping for ACA health plans in the federal marketplace begins Nov. 1, and an analysis by the health care research organization KFF found those shoppers will face median proposed premium increases of 15%. Many people who get insurance through work will also start seeing in October and November how much more will come out of their paychecks next year.

And while the GOP polling may have identified some winning messages, a new KFF survey released Tuesday suggests voters are not really absorbing them. The poll of more than 1,000 Americans found Democrats holding a 42% to 22% edge over Republicans for which party they trust more to handle health care costs. That is a dramatic jump since April, when Democrats had a 37% to 26% lead.

Liz Hamel of KFF told The Sun that Republican messaging on fraud, waste and abuse has resonated with voters but doesn’t necessarily translate to a belief that prioritizing fraud will lower their costs.

She added that Republicans’ historical advantage on the economy had sometimes extended to health, even as voters favored Democrats on programs such as Medicare and Medicaid. But that has recently changed.

“We're finding that Democrats even have an edge on health care costs among voters,” she said.

Whether Republicans can turn their health care pitches into greater voter trust remains an open question, even if there is not much time left before the midterm elections. Burgess said that trust ultimately depends on results.

“Parties do own issues, but ownership isn't a deed. It's a lease, and it renews on performance,” he said.
entries.author: Kadia Goba

entries.title: Trump Says He’s Reviewing Top Advisers’ Work for Far-Right Balkan Government
entries.summary: “If there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Wednesday he was looking into reports that two of his top political advisers had performed consulting work for a pro-Russian nationalist government in Bosnia-Herzegovina, suggesting that he may fire both longtime confidants if there is a conflict of interest.

The comments followed a bombshell report in The New York Times that Chris LaCivita and James Blair traveled to Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, shortly before its elections on Sunday to advise the government on voting-related matters. Each was paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the work, the Times reported.

Trump defended the arrangement in a post on Truth Social, saying both men are outside consultants and are allowed to work for other clients.

“They do not work for me, other than as outside consultants. They most likely have numerous clients,” he said, adding that he planned to ask them for an accounting of their client list.

“If there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” Trump added.

The president later addressed the situation during a press conference in the Oval Office, insisting that there was likely no conflict of interest because they do not work directly in the White House. 

“They're not sitting around a Cabinet table or anything like that,” he said, adding: “I'm sure they have many clients, but that would be true with everybody in Washington.”

Both men hold prominent roles in Trump’s political operation ahead of next month’s midterm elections. LaCivita co-managed Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, while Blair served as his political director and later as a White House deputy chief of staff. Blair has since taken a leading role in executing Trump’s midterm strategy.

Republika Srpska is governed by the nationalist SNSD, the party of longtime Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik, who has maintained close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The Trump administration lifted U.S. sanctions on Dodik, his family members and several allies in October 2025.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: Rubio’s State Department Pushes Russia for More Info on Lab Worker’s Death
entries.summary: It warned Moscow that withholding details on a potential infectious disease was a failure to comply with international agreements.
entries.content:
U.S. officials warned Russia that it was failing to comply with global health obligations by not sharing details about the death of a plague researcher in Siberia. The pressure from the Americans came in the form of a confidential diplomatic communication, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.

Following the death of 28-year-old lab worker Daria Shipilova, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for Moscow to release more details about what made her sick.

“We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that we can react accordingly and appropriately,” Rubio told reporters on Tuesday. “But we're gonna have to make those decisions on the basis of the information that we're learning and being provided, and so far that is still quite limited.”

The mysterious circumstances around the death has prompted Russian officials to quarantine a reported 200 people.

President Donald Trump said Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin “soon.”

The secrecy surrounding the potential infectious disease is the latest sore spot between the U.S. and Russia. Trump had said he’d negotiate an end to Putin’s war in Ukraine on the first day of his second term. Two years later, the fighting appears no closer to resolution. And while the president signed into law a sweeping Russia sanctions bill last month, his administration also faced backlash for inviting Putin to the G20 summit in Miami later this year.

“We haven't ended Russia-Ukraine yet," Trump said at a Tuesday event in Baltimore. “I'm working on that one, that one I thought would be the easiest one for me. But … that's going to happen too pretty soon.”

When asked for comment, representatives for the White House and State Department referred The Washington Sun to Trump and Rubio’s comments.

A 2005 global health pact called the International Health Regulations requires countries that experience an event that could become an international public health emergency to notify the World Health Organization within 24 hours, provide updates and share lab results.

While Moscow has provided some information to WHO, The Wall Street Journal reported, it hasn’t provided detailed answers required by the agreement.

Russian authorities said Shipilova, who worked at Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died suddenly of pneumonia earlier this month. With gaps in the information coming out of Russia, some public health officials worry her illness could have been caused by a deadly pathogen present in her lab work.

Russia has denied those claims.

Russia’s national public health agency told Russian media on Monday that after a comprehensive analysis of Shipilova’s body, they found “no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities.” It added in a separate statement to the Russian News Agency that evidence of COVID-19 and a cold virus had been found among the people being quarantined.

The WHO has stated there’s a low risk that the disease that killed the lab worker would spread globally. Trump ordered the U.S. to withdraw from the international health organization upon his return to the White House, citing what he called the organization’s “mishandling” of the pandemic that began during his first term.

The U.S. Embassy in Russia on Tuesday warned Americans in the country of the increased health risk and said the American government would have limited ability to help citizens there.
entries.author: Andrea Padilla

entries.title: Hillary Clinton Endorses Her First Candidate of 2026
entries.summary: The former first lady and secretary of state endorsed Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan in her run for U.S. Senate.
entries.content:
Hillary Clinton endorsed her first candidate of the 2026 election cycle this week.

The former first lady and secretary of state endorsed Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a Democrat, in her Senate run against Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter and commentator.

Clinton announced the endorsement on Tuesday, her first midterm endorsement for a House or Senate candidate.

“Peggy Flanagan has spent her career fighting for children and families, from the Children's Defense Fund to the Lieutenant Governor's office, and she's delivered for them,” Clinton said in a statement. “I know she'll be that same champion in the Senate, and I’m proud to endorse her.”

Clinton also criticized President Donald Trump amid rising prices.

"Donald Trump has made it harder for families to afford childcare, groceries, and health care for their kids. His tariffs and war in Iran are driving up prices, and his budget ripped health care and food assistance away from children so billionaires could get another tax cut,” she said.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a statement, Flanagan said she was “honored” to have Clinton’s endorsement.

“Secretary Clinton has spent five decades fighting for those families, and I'm honored to have her support as we take that fight to the United States Senate,” Flanagan wrote.

Several high-profile politicians have endorsed Flanagan, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders and Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar.

Clinton began her career at the Children's Defense Fund, where she worked as a staff attorney and chaired the organization’s board. Between 2001 and 2009, she served as a U.S. senator for New York, and she ran for president in 2008 and 2016.

Flanagan previously served as the head of Children’s Defense Fund in Minnesota, where she co-chaired a campaign to raise the minimum wage and index it to inflation.

“Long before she was First Lady, Senator, or Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton was knocking on doors for the Children's Defense Fund, making the case that every child in this country deserves a fair shot. That same work shaped me,” Flanagan said in her statement.
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: Trump Wants a New Camp David at His West Palm Beach Golf Club
entries.summary: Under a new plan, part of the county-owned property would be provided to the federal government, while the rest would remain a private golf course.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump wants to build a permanent Camp David-style presidential retreat at his golf club in West Palm Beach, Florida, according to a letter a lawyer for the property sent last month to local officials.

And the county is seriously considering his proposal, County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo told The Washington Post. He said officials are in contact with the General Services Administration and have begun plans to identify a parcel for the project.

Palm Beach County owns the land beneath Trump International Golf Club West Palm Beach and leases it to Trump's company, the Trump Organization.

Under the terms listed in the letter, the Trump Organization would continue operating the course next to the presidential compound and keep making lease payments to the county. Representatives for Trump told county officials last week that the government-owned retreat would have a separate entrance from the private club.

No final agreement with the federal government has been announced.

The Palm Beach Post first reported the proposal last month after Harvey Oyer, a lawyer representing Trump International Golf Club, sent a letter to county commissioners outlining plans for a permanent presidential golf course. The newspaper later reported that county staff had begun exploring the proposal.

Under the plan, part of the county-owned property would be provided to the federal government for a presidential residence and related facilities, while the rest would remain a private golf course. Oyer said Trump would pay to build the presidential facilities.

The site could host future presidents, foreign leaders and international summits. Future presidents would also receive complimentary memberships to the Trump-owned club.

“Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County,” Oyer wrote to county commissioners last month.

Oyer said construction would not be completed before Trump leaves office and called the project “a gift” to Trump’s successors.

“My understanding is that President Trump views this as a lasting contribution to the presidency and to those who will hold the office after him,” Abruzzo told the Post.

A White House official told the Post that the property offered several advantages for presidential use, including its proximity to an airport and law enforcement, existing security features and the lack of homes and large buildings immediately surrounding the course.

Trump reported $36.9 million in earnings from the West Palm Beach club in his most recent financial disclosure.

The Florida retreat would not replace Camp David. Presidents have used the government-owned Maryland compound for decades as a getaway from Washington and a venue for meetings with foreign leaders.

Trump has generally chosen his own properties when spending time away from Washington. He has also been dismissive of the Maryland retreat in the past, once saying its appeal would wear off after about half an hour.

Another Trump-owned club in Palm Beach, Mar-a-Lago, was once intended for a similar purpose. Marjorie Merriweather Post arranged for the estate to become a federal presidential retreat, but the government later returned it to the Post Foundation following her death. Trump bought the property in 1985.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: U.S. Military Bans Booze for Soldiers in Okinawa After a Marine Was Accused of Murder
entries.summary: Also included in the order was a 48-hour pause on operations and mandatory discussions on off-duty behavior and Okinawan culture.
entries.content:
The U.S. military is instituting a 48-hour alcohol ban for soldiers stationed in Okinawa after a Marine was accused of murdering a 39-year-old Japanese woman, setting off an international incident that has inflamed tensions between the two countries.

The “Period of Training,” as military leaders called it, will run from Wednesday to Friday. Also included in the order was a 48-hour pause on operations and mandatory discussions on off-duty behavior, enforcement mechanisms, alcohol awareness, Okinawan culture and alliance responsibilities, according to a memo written by Lt. Gen. Benjamin T. Watson, the Okinawa area coordinator and commanding general of III Marine Expeditionary Force, and posted to social media Tuesday evening.

The alcohol restriction applies to private residences, Watson noted. Bases will remain open for mission-essential and essential personal movement, according to an FAQ page.

Watson said the opportunity would allow military officials to train service members on standards, discipline and responsibilities as “members of the Okinawan community.”

“Every member of this force must understand that individual conduct has consequences,” wrote Watson.

Following the training, service members will enter a 30-day “Period of Reflection.” During that time, the military will implement restrictions on service members to remind them that “liberty is a privilege and a collective responsibility.”

Additionally, service members must follow a midnight curfew and are required to be back on base in their assigned quarters or off-base housing from midnight to 5 a.m., the memo states.

The military will also implement enhanced supervision at gates across all installations on Okinawa. Officials have not released details on what the enhanced security measures would entail.

A review of liberty policies and procedures will also be conducted, and recommendations will be shared with the Okinawa Area Coordinating Committee for potential implementation.

It’s unclear if alcohol consumption will be allowed during the reflection period.

In response to a question about why force-wide measures are being directed, the U.S. military said: “Incidents of this nature demand a pause for reflection. Every interaction with the people of Okinawa either builds or undermines the trust essential to our alliance.”

Officials arrested 20-year-old Devin Jacob Ballard on Sunday in connection with the murder of Anna Yagi. Okinawa police believe Ballard strangled Yagi in a Naha hotel room Saturday and stole her personal items, The Associated Press reported.

Ballard, who was based at Futenma Air Station, has denied the allegations, local outlets reported.

Okinawa is home to 32 U.S. Military bases. The U.S. has maintained an active military presence in the region since 1945. More than 50,000 American troops are stationed in Japan under a bilateral security agreement, according to The Associated Press.

The ongoing military presence in Okinawa has been a long-standing source of frustration for the local community, the AP reported. About 70% of the U.S. military’s presence in Japan is concentrated on the island.

However, some residents view it as a valuable asset in response to ongoing threats from China, according to the outlet.

The murder has nonetheless raised new questions about the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, with local leaders taking aim at the two countries’ security agreements.

On Wednesday, Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja told reporters, “The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases,” according to a translation published by the AP.

“It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged,” he added.
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: Ken Paxton Audio Keeps Leaking: Now It's His Frustrations Over Iran
entries.summary: Audio of the private admission was reported just before Paxton is expected to appear with President Donald Trump at a San Antonio rally.
entries.content:
Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee in Texas, told donors and lobbyists he believes the war in Iran and high gas prices have hurt his campaign.

His comments, in which he said he doesn’t “know what’s behind some of the decisions,” were made in a private gathering held in Washington, D.C., on Sept. 24 and reported by Axios on Wednesday. It’s the third leak that’s emerged from the fundraiser, drawing scrutiny to the candidate in a race that is increasingly seen as promising for Democrats.

“So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable,” Paxton can be heard saying in the latest clip, adding that affordability is “by far our biggest problem.”

“It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel,” Paxton said. “When it’s over $6 per gallon for diesel … people are feeling the pinch.”

The latest report was published ahead of a campaign rally on Wednesday in San Antonio, where Paxton is expected to appear alongside President Donald Trump.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, Madison Cercy, a campaign spokesperson for Paxton, said that the audio is a “non-story.”

“The Attorney General said what every Texan already knows: gas and diesel prices are too high, and hardworking Texans are struggling at the pump and at the grocery store," Cercy said. "President Trump is doing everything he can to bring prices down, and Ken Paxton is going to Washington to help him by putting money back in families' pockets."

In other clips from the September meeting, obtained by The New York Times and Politico, Paxton told donors that his polling numbers were hurt by the GOP midterm convention hosted in Dallas last month and said his campaign’s direction was driven by establishment figures.

“I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming, you know, from D.C.,” Paxton said in the audio obtained by Politico earlier this week. “I don’t control the message or what we’re doing.”

James Talarico, the Democratic nominee in the Texas Senate race, briefly responded to Paxton’s remark on social media.

“Ken Paxton is a puppet,” Talarico said.

On Tuesday, Trump told reporters he hadn’t heard Paxton’s comments.

“Ken and everyone is doing much better now that I’ve started the rallies,” Trump said. “It’s brought a whole new awareness to how great the economy is doing.”

The topic of affordability has created a rift between Trump and some Republicans ahead of the November midterms. The president has repeatedly referred to concerns over inflation and prices as a “hoax,” but voters across the country have signaled that economic issues are top of mind.

When speaking with donors, Paxton suggested that one of his campaign proposals, which includes write-offs for housing, health care and family-related expenses, is one way he would address the issue.

"I'm just trying to figure out ways I can help people,” he said. “That's the only way: I can propose legislation.”
entries.author: Emma Ruby
